subject: chemistry
question_text: Alkali metals and their salts impart characteristic colours to an oxidising flame. Explain the reason.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.87, chapter 7 s-BLOCK ELEMENTS, SAQ question 29. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. This book prints no exam-appearance years for this chapter, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The flame colours printed here — lithium crimson red, sodium golden yellow, potassium pale violet, rubidium reddish violet, caesium blue — are the source book's own table and agree with the standard values; potassium is violet and sodium is the yellow one, and that pairing was checked deliberately because it is the one most often reversed.

steps.label: What is observed
lines: An oxidising flame is the non-luminous
flame of a Bunsen burner.
When an alkali metal or one of its salts
is heated in this flame, the flame takes
a colour that belongs to that metal.
This is the basis of the flame test used
in qualitative analysis.
steps.why: The question asks for a reason, so the thing to be explained must be stated first; naming the oxidising flame also fixes the condition, because the colour is seen in the hot non-luminous flame and not in a smoky one.
common_mistakes: Saying only the free metal gives the colour. The salts of the metal give the same colour.
Describing the colour of the burning gas. The colour comes from the metal, not from the fuel.
steps.memory_tip: The colour belongs to the metal, whether it is taken as the metal or as its salt.
steps.margin_note: State what is observed before explaining why it happens.

steps.label: The electron is excited
lines: An alkali metal atom has a single
electron in its outermost ns orbital.
That electron is far from the nucleus,
is screened by the inner shells and is
loosely held, so the ionisation enthalpy
is low.
The heat of the flame is enough to raise
this electron to a higher energy level.
steps.why: Excitation is possible only because the single ns¹ electron is weakly held; a metal whose valence electron is tightly bound is not excited by a flame at all, which is why the alkali metals show this behaviour so clearly.
common_mistakes: Saying the flame removes the electron from the atom. The electron is raised to a higher level, not knocked out.
Saying an inner-shell electron is excited. It is the single outermost ns¹ electron.
steps.memory_tip: One loosely held ns¹ electron, so a Bunsen flame is hot enough to excite it.
steps.margin_note: Name the electron that is excited: the single outermost ns¹ electron.

steps.label: Light emitted on falling back
lines: The excited electron is not stable and
falls back to the lower energy level.
The energy difference is given out as
radiation:

lines.text: ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν = hc / λ

lines: Each metal has its own energy gap, so
each emits its own wavelength.
That wavelength lies in the visible
region, so a colour is seen.
steps.why: The light is emitted while the electron RETURNS, not while it is being excited, and the energy gap is fixed for each metal — that is what makes the colour characteristic and lets one metal be told from another.
common_mistakes: Saying light is emitted when the electron is excited. It is emitted when the electron falls back.
Leaving out the energy relation. ΔE = hν is what links the energy gap to the colour seen.
steps.memory_tip: Heat sends the electron up; light is given out when it comes down.
steps.margin_note: The relation ΔE = hν belongs in this step.

steps.label: The characteristic colours
lines: The colours down the group are:

lines.text: The colour seen names the metal

steps.why: The reason explains why any colour appears; the list is what shows that the colour differs from metal to metal, and a reason without the list leaves the word characteristic in the question unanswered.
common_mistakes: Giving potassium a yellow flame. Potassium is pale violet and sodium is the golden yellow one.
Saying all the alkali metals give one colour. Each has its own energy gap and its own colour.
steps.memory_tip: Sodium is the yellow one; potassium is the violet one.
steps.margin_note: Give the colours in order down the group.

insider_note: Write both halves: why a colour appears at all, and which colour belongs to which metal — potassium is pale violet and sodium is golden yellow.
